title: Allergic Rhinitis and Sinusitis: Separate Inflammation from Bacterial Disease
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis and acute rhinosinusitis are usually inflammatory or viral syndromes, not automatic antibiotic indications. Identify allergic triggers and chronicity, use intranasal corticosteroid and supportive therapy appropriately, and reserve antibiotics or urgent ENT evaluation for a convincing bacterial complication or red-flag presentation.
recognize: Allergic rhinitis often causes sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea and nasal/ocular symptoms linked to exposures or seasons.
Acute viral rhinosinusitis commonly causes congestion, facial pressure and discharge that improve without antibiotics.
differentiate: Bacterial rhinosinusitis is more likely with severe or persistent/worsening illness patterns rather than discharge colour alone.
Unilateral bleeding, mass, severe orbital symptoms, neurologic signs or recurrent focal disease require a different diagnostic pathway.
assessment: Assess duration and trajectory, allergy/exposure pattern, fever/severity, facial/dental pain, asthma, medication use, pregnancy and red flags such as orbital swelling or severe headache.
workup: Typical allergic rhinitis and uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis are clinical diagnoses; routine CT and sinus radiographs are not indicated.
Use imaging or specialty evaluation for suspected orbital/intracranial complication, mass, recurrent atypical disease or surgical planning.
management: Use allergen reduction, saline and intranasal corticosteroid therapy for allergic rhinitis when appropriate; add antihistamine based on symptom profile.
Use supportive care for uncomplicated viral rhinosinusitis and current Canadian/local antibiotic guidance only when bacterial disease is clinically supported.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestants can cause rebound congestion with prolonged use.
Review sedating antihistamine burden, hypertension/pregnancy considerations and duplicate OTC cold products.
redFlags: Orbital swelling or painful eye movement
Severe frontal headache or neurologic signs
Unilateral persistent obstruction/bleeding or mass concern
counselling: Explain that coloured mucus alone does not prove bacterial infection and that nasal steroid benefit requires regular correct technique.
followUp: Reassess persistent or recurrent symptoms, confirm adherence/technique and investigate structural or alternative diagnoses when the expected course does not occur.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because nasal discharge is green without considering duration, trajectory, severity or complications.
oneLinePearl: Rhinitis is usually inflammation; sinus antibiotics need a bacterial pattern, not a mucus colour.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory/ENT antimicrobial stewardship
Canadian allergy and primary-care rhinosinusitis practice principles

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Decide Who Needs Imaging and Antibiotics
bottomLine: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and does not benefit from routine antibiotics. The NP task is to identify features that increase pneumonia probability—abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings, hypoxemia, frailty or systemic illness—and use chest imaging selectively when the result changes diagnosis or disposition.
recognize: Acute bronchitis commonly causes cough, sometimes with sputum or transient wheeze, after an upper-respiratory syndrome.
Pneumonia probability rises with fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles/bronchial breath sounds, pleuritic pain or systemic illness.
differentiate: Purulent sputum does not reliably distinguish bacterial pneumonia from viral bronchitis.
COPD/asthma exacerbation, PE, heart failure, influenza/COVID and pertussis can present with acute cough and require different management.
assessment: Assess respiratory rate, temperature, oxygen saturation, heart rate, work of breathing, focal chest findings, comorbidity, frailty, aspiration risk and symptom trajectory.
workup: Do not order chest radiography routinely when vitals and lung examination make pneumonia unlikely in a stable ambulatory patient.
Obtain chest imaging when pneumonia is clinically plausible, the patient is higher risk or the result will change treatment/disposition.
management: Treat uncomplicated acute bronchitis with reassurance, hydration/symptom care and return precautions rather than routine antibiotics.
Treat confirmed or strongly suspected pneumonia using current local Canadian guidance and disposition based on severity.
medicationSafety: Avoid antibiotic exposure that adds allergy, C. difficile, interaction and resistance risk without benefit.
Avoid routine opioid cough suppressants, especially in older adults or patients using other sedatives.
redFlags: Failure to improve or worsening after an expected viral course
counselling: Explain that cough from bronchitis can persist for weeks and that antibiotics do not shorten most viral bronchitis.
Give clear return instructions for dyspnea, persistent fever, confusion, dehydration or worsening symptoms.
followUp: Reassess if the clinical course deviates from expected bronchitis recovery and reconsider pneumonia or another diagnosis rather than repeating empiric antibiotics.
examTrap: Treating purulent sputum as proof of bacterial infection or ordering chest X-ray for every uncomplicated acute cough.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is a cough syndrome; pneumonia requires a lower-respiratory disease pattern and sometimes imaging.
